chunks: From him, from Muhammad al-Katib, from Abdullah ibn Ali ibn Umar ibn Yazid, from his uncle Muhammad ibn Umar, that he wrote to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who died and was a mawla (client/freedman) of a man, and his master had died before him, and the mawla had a son and daughters, so I asked him about the inheritance of the mawla, and he said:
"It is for the men, not the women." Ali said: "And this is also contrary to what our companions hold."

27 - And - Al-Rida (peace be upon him) wrote to Muhammad ibn Sinan in his reply to his questions: "The reason for giving women half of what is given to men in inheritance is that when the woman marries she takes (dowry), and the man gives, so therefore it was increased for the men."
ai.seo_question: What is the reason for men receiving double the inheritance share of women in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a specific juristic nuance regarding the inheritance of a *mawla* (client) whose patron predeceased him, noting that the inheritance passes to sons to the exclusion of daughters—a ruling that some scholars consider contrary to the general consensus of the Shia school. Complementing this, Imam al-Rida elucidates the underlying wisdom (*illa*) for the standard male-to-female inheritance ratio, linking the man's larger share to his obligatory financial responsibilities, such as providing the dowry (*mahr*) and maintenance, whereas the woman retains her share without such burdens.
